Steland

Two days before the new cabinet's first meeting, the state printing office sent proofs for approval. One read 'Republic of Stelander'. On the other, in the same typeface, stood a word that had not appeared on official seals for generations: 'Steland'.

The dispute was not about spelling. In the old highland documents, Steland was the country's name. The form 'Stelander' denoted a person or thing belonging to Steland. For decades, foreign chancelleries had written of the Stelander government, the Stelander administration and Stelander territories. After the Fada Pact, the modifier gradually became a noun. The Party established it as the name of its new order, as though the end of the war had brought a new country into existence.

Shabrat studied both sheets for a long time. He had no intention of claiming that the past decades had never happened. But the independence won after the civil war did not need a name that had grown out of a foreign chancellery and been adopted by its own regime. The new cabinet was not restoring a tribal union or a bygone century. It was restoring the country's right to name itself.

The head of the printing office asked which version should go to press.
Print 'Steland'.
The Archive That Survived the War

Combat engineers had to force open the archive vault's door. The retreating administration had removed the sign and taken part of the card index, but the fire never reached the basement. Decades of Ivanov's state remained on the shelves.

Within the first few hours, they found things the resistance had previously known only through rumour. Annexes to the Fada Pact omitted from the public version. Lists of Nodrulian advisers with access to the ministries. Transfers of rights to mines and water. The High Houses' secret accounts. Registers of detainees in which some names ended with the terse note 'transferred', although their families had received no news for years.

Several of Shabrat's people proposed taking the documents straight to the journalists. After the war, the country wanted one great admission that everything the underground had said was true. Shabrat refused. First, every folder had to be numbered, copied, traced to its source, and every signature identified. Publication would follow only then.

For decades, the old regime had replaced history with a convenient story. It would be all too easy for the new state to do the same in reverse. If Steland intended to try people and revise treaties, it needed more than the victors' legends. It needed documents that would outlast the next government too.
No document without a number.
Monument to the Father of Peace

The crane arrived in the square early in the morning, although no one had ordered the monument's removal. The municipal service had decided that, after a change of government, it was better to be ready. By noon, resistance veterans, officials, journalists and several dozen residents had gathered around the bronze Ivanov.

Someone had already written 'capitulation' on the pedestal. Nearby, an elderly woman laid flowers. Her son had survived the final year of bombardment precisely because the Fada Pact was signed. A few metres away, a young soldier in Shabrat's army was showing his comrades his grandfather's name on a list of people who disappeared during the post-war purges.

Neither side was entirely lying. Ivanov had ended a war Steland could barely continue. He had also built an order in which peace gradually became a justification for foreign influence, secret agreements and the Chamber's power. Tearing down the statue was easier than deciding which of these two histories should remain in the square.

The workers stopped the crane and waited for instructions. For the first time, Ivanov's own apparatus would not decide how he was remembered.
Keep the monument. Replace the plaque.
